$comment: Rules about presenting a range of outcomes rather than one, and about saying honestly what the range does and does not cover. Standards 19 and 20. All four are `document` with `assurance: partial`, and the reason is uncomfortable enough to state plainly: everything a checker can see about a scenario set is its shape, and everything that makes a scenario set worth reading is its content.
$admissionTest: Standard 19 R3 — whether the adverse case is genuinely adverse — is deliberately NOT given an id here. It is already asked by risk.adverse-case-is-a-loss under Standard 16, and asking it twice under two ids would raise `frameworkCoverage` without checking anything more. Standard 20 R2 is likewise carried by math.projection-precision and the forbidden-level prohibited.excessive-precision. What was refused admission outright is named in each standard: R6's recommended responses, R2's reasoned omissions, R5's decision-relevance of a wide range, and R1's grammar-of-fact test — the last kept out because a rule that cannot tell "your contributions will total $60,000" from "your portfolio will be worth $663,000" fails correct documents.

rules.title: A projecting document presents all four named scenarios
rules.description: A document containing projection language presents scenario labels corresponding to all four the source names: conservative, base, optimistic, and adverse.
rules.rationale: A partial set is a chosen set, and the member most often missing is the adverse one. Fixing the four labels removes the discretion over which cases get shown, which is the discretion that produces a document showing only what goes right.
rules.remediation: Present all four scenarios with the same detail as the base case, or name the omitted one and explain why it does not apply here.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that four LABELS are PRESENT, never that the scenarios behind them are ADEQUATE. A table headed conservative / base / optimistic / adverse whose four figures are 6.5%, 7%, 7.5% and 6% passes completely while violating Standard 19 R3 entirely; that question is carried by risk.adverse-case-is-a-loss, which is manual-review and claims no assurance. A document with no projection language reports NOT_EVALUATED rather than passing, because a detector that finds no projections must not thereby grant an exemption.

rules.title: The document states that its scenarios do not exhaust possible outcomes
rules.description: A document presenting a scenario set carries an explicit statement that outcomes outside the set — including worse ones — are possible.
rules.rationale: A bounded set of scenarios reads as a bounded set of futures, and the adverse case reads as the worst case. The statement is what stops the absence of an outcome from the analysis standing, in the reader's mind, as evidence of its impossibility.
rules.remediation: State plainly, where the set is presented rather than in a footer, that the scenarios are illustrative and that outcomes worse than the adverse case can occur.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that the SENTENCE is present, never that the document behaves as though it were true: a page carrying the disclaimer and then drawing a confident conclusion bounded by its own adverse case passes. Whether an outcome was omitted for a reason or for convenience is not reachable from the text at all, which is why Standard 19 keeps that requirement in prose.

rules.title: Projected values are expressed as ranges rather than single figures
rules.description: A document stating projected values expresses them as ranges or distributions rather than as single determinate figures.
rules.rationale: A point estimate carries an implicit claim to precision the method cannot support, and readers act on the number rather than on the uncertainty around it. The range is the result of the analysis; the midpoint is a summary of it that discards the part the reader most needs.
rules.remediation: Replace the single figure with the range the scenario set actually produces, and round both ends to a precision the assumptions support.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural: it establishes that range language or paired figures are PRESENT where projections appear, never that the range is HONEST. A range of 6.9% to 7.1% satisfies every check a machine can run and none of the purpose, and a document that presents a range and then reasons throughout from its midpoint passes cleanly.

rules.title: The source of the uncertainty is named and its kind distinguished
rules.description: A document disclosing uncertainty says what is uncertain, distinguishing uncertainty in the inputs from uncertainty in the model's structure.
rules.rationale: The two are remedied differently: input uncertainty narrows with better data, structural uncertainty does not narrow at all. A document that blurs them implies the second is the first, and therefore implies it will go away with more work.
rules.remediation: Name the uncertain inputs and their plausible ranges separately from the structural assumptions the model makes, and say which of the two dominates the result.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that uncertainty LANGUAGE is present and that both kinds are named, never that the disclosure is ADEQUATE: a sentence reading "there is of course model risk" satisfies this rule and tells the reader nothing about which part of the model is doubted or what would follow if it were wrong.
